Charleston at a glance

Charleston, seat of Charleston County, is South Carolina's largest city by population. It had 150,227 residents in the 2020 census and an estimated 159,423 in 2025. The wider metro area across Berkeley, Charleston and Dorchester counties was estimated at 849,417 in 2023.

Think of it as several markets under one name. Downtown is the Peninsula, with the Ashley River on one side and the Cooper on the other. Inside the city limits you will also find West Ashley, James Island, Johns Island, the Cainhoy Peninsula and Daniel Island. Two houses with a Charleston address can sit under different rules and attract different buyers.

Older houses and repair lists

The city dates to 1670, and plenty of its housing is old enough to need work. An 1886 earthquake damaged about 2,000 buildings, and Hurricane Hugo struck on September 21, 1989. Local inspectors and buyers study foundations, roofs, wiring and any history of water damage.

Putting off repairs makes a standard listing slower. Financed buyers tend to send a repair request after inspection, and some lenders hesitate over homes in rough shape. Demand comes from people relocating for work, investors and second-home shoppers, yet a poorly kept home or one in a bad flood zone is a tough fit for a typical mortgage buyer.

Flood zones and permits

For many Charleston homes, flooding is the largest condition problem. Elevation is roughly 3 feet, almost half of annual rainfall arrives in summer, and hurricane season runs from summer into early fall.

Charleston's floodplain program affects what you can fix before a sale. Painting, interior finishes and storm repairs all require a permit if the property lies in a Special Flood Hazard Area. That designation covers AE, Coastal A and VE zones, where the yearly flood chance is 1 percent or higher. Points worth knowing:

  • New construction in the hazard area has had to be designed 2 feet over Base Flood Elevation since July 1, 2020, with residential substantial improvements required to clear it by 1 foot.
  • Building types 1A, 1B, 2A and 3 built as slab-on-grade are barred from the 100-year floodplain for applications filed from January 1, 2024.
  • Coastal A Zone design rules have applied to new construction and substantial improvements since January 1, 2023.
  • FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 started with new flood policies on October 1, 2021 and with renewals on April 1, 2022.

Email floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov for elevation certificates and hazard details. Get them early: an insurance quote can move a buyer's offer. Further detail sits on the floodplain management page and the flood zone permit page.

Can a buyer run a short-term rental in a Charleston house?

Sometimes. Charleston groups short-term rentals into location-based categories, and a property gets only one rental unit in any of them.

  • Category 1: the Old and Historic District on the peninsula, limited to existing structures individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Category 2: the remainder of the peninsula outside the overlay, limited to buildings at least 50 years old.
  • Category 3: areas off the peninsula, among them Daniel Island, James Island, Johns Island and West Ashley.

Each category adds a requirement of one more off-street space measuring 9 feet by 18 feet 6 inches, beyond ordinary zoning parking. For a single-family home the total is 3 spaces. Commercially zoned property in the overlay may qualify for a Commercial Short Term Rental Permit, and residential property for a Bed and Breakfast Permit. Reach the city at shorttermrental@charleston-sc.gov or 843-724-7311, or read the category criteria page.

Was the house a short-term rental? Tell buyers which permit it carries, since a buyer counting on that income will ask to see it.

Deed recording fee

Under Code section 12-24-10, the state's deed recording fee is $1.85 per $500 of the price, rounding up for any remainder. Here is how it divides.

Who receives itFee per $500 of value
State$1.30
County$0.55
Total$1.85

Responsibility for paying falls first on the seller, then on the buyer if the seller does not. An affidavit of value goes in with the deed, though the register of deeds may waive it. Certain transfers are exempt, such as a deed given in lieu of foreclosure; the affidavit then names the exemption. Read the law at scstatehouse.gov. Recording and tax dates are set locally, so check with the county offices.

Property tax and what changes after a sale

Assessment ratios in South Carolina are 4 percent for a legal residence the owner lives in and 6 percent for everything else. The lower ratio covers the house plus as many as five adjoining acres, provided it is rented no more than 72 days a year.

An investor who buys and rents the place generally does not qualify for the 4 percent ratio, so the bill can go up after the sale. Reassessment happens at least every fifth year, and a change of $1,000 or more in value must be sent to the owner in a notice (Code sections 12-43-217 and 12-43-220). Call the treasurer for your balance before closing day. If you still owe a bill when the house sells, the closing attorney normally pays it from your proceeds, so ask for the figure early rather than at the table. Also ask the assessor which ratio your own bill uses today, because a mistake there is easy to fix before a sale and harder afterward.

Choosing between a listing and a cash sale

Charleston sellers commonly hit one of these snags, and each steers toward a different way to sell.

  • Repairs in a flood zone that need a permit first.
  • Aging buildings with postponed work on the roof, plumbing or wiring.
  • Inherited homes, where every heir has to agree before signing.
  • Rentals with a tenant or permit question still open.

Listing works for a well-kept house when you can live with showings. Selling for cash works better when repairs, permits or a firm deadline rule out months on the market. Cash buyers usually take the house as-is, which removes repair haggling, the appraisal and any wait for a lender.

Before choosing, pull together your flood zone and elevation certificate, permit records for past work or rental use, and the payoff amount on your mortgage. For an inherited house, add the documents showing who may sign. With those on hand, the gap between offer and closing shrinks.

Frequently asked questions

What is the main flood rule when I sell a house in Charleston?

Work of any kind in a Special Flood Hazard Area needs a city permit, storm repairs included. Residential substantial improvements there must rise 1 foot above Base Flood Elevation as of July 1, 2020. Request your elevation certificate from the floodplain office prior to pricing.

How is the South Carolina deed fee figured on a Charleston sale?

The rate is $1.85 for each $500 or fraction of the sale value, split $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county. The seller owes it first; the buyer is a backstop. Your closing attorney will state the actual amount.

Can I rent my Charleston house short term after buying it?

Possibly. All three city categories permit a single short-term rental unit per property and add a parking requirement. On the peninsula, categories 1 and 2 turn on location and building age. Check with the city first.

Does selling to a cash buyer change flood or permit duties?

No. Permits, disclosure and the deed fee apply whichever way the house sells. What a cash sale removes is the financing wait and the repair requests, which is the real difference for most sellers.

Where can I find Charleston County tax dates?

Contact the county auditor, assessor and treasurer. State law makes January 15 the final penalty-free payment day for most bills, while notices and appeal windows shift by cycle, so phone the offices.

Columbia at a glance

Columbia is the state capital and the county seat of Richland County. Some of its territory lies in Lexington and Kershaw counties, so confirm which county holds your parcel first. The answer tells you whose assessor and treasurer to call.

Columbia sits mid-state on the fall line, and the Broad and Saluda rivers merge here into the Congaree. A parcel near any of them should get a flood zone check. Columbia was laid out as a planned capital in 1786, and burned in part in 1865, so one street can hold a historic bungalow and the next a postwar ranch. Condition and price vary block by block, and a citywide average tells you little.

Rental permits and short-term rentals

A Residential Rental Permit must be in hand before any tenant occupies a residential rental in the city. The rule covers units rented after July 1, 2016, and permits expire each year on December 31.

  • The nonbusiness form is for owners of up to 4 units, and the business form for owners of 5 or more.
  • Applications go to Code Enforcement at 920 Hemlock Drive, Columbia, SC 29201, and you pay online once approved.
  • For questions, call 803-545-4362.

Short-term rentals follow separate rules. An operator needs an STR Permit from Code Enforcement plus a Business License. Under Ordinance 2025-107, STRs are allowed in mixed-use, activity center and corridor, commercial and employment campus districts. In residential districts they are allowed on parcels fronting a four-lane arterial or collector street. An ordinance approved March 3, 2026 lets owner-occupied homes in residential districts operate without the four-lane condition. The city explains the rules on its STR page and the residential rentals page.

Selling with tenants in place? Renew the permit first. Any buyer or investor will want to see it, and a lapsed one is better fixed before you list.

Property tax due dates and penalties

In this state the counties, not the cities, send and collect property tax bills. For a house inside Columbia, the value comes from the Richland County Assessor. You can pay from September 30 through January 15, and late charges build in stages after that (Code sections 12-45-70 and 12-45-180).

If still unpaid byAdded penalty
After January 153 percent

Your notice carries the exact amount and date, and the treasurer can confirm both. Should you sell partway through the year, the closing attorney usually settles what is owed out of your proceeds.

How to appeal your assessment

Disagree with your Richland County value? Put the objection in writing, either through the online portal or at the counter, and attach evidence for the figure you think is right. Time runs out 90 days after the date printed on the reassessment notice, or on the first penalty date of the current bill if that is sooner. You still owe the bill while the appeal is pending.

A representative filing on your behalf must hold a power of attorney on Form SC2848. When the owner is an LLC, include its organizing documents.

The Assessor's Office is at 2020 Hampton Street, Suite 2058, Columbia, SC 29204, phone 803-576-2640. The county's assessment appeal page has the online portal. A lower assessed value helps whoever owns the house next, yet it seldom moves today's sale price, so weigh the effort against your timeline.

What buyers notice about a Columbia house

Hot summers put air conditioning, attic ventilation and the roof under the inspector's spotlight in Columbia. Anything near the Broad, Saluda or Congaree rivers should come with a flood zone determination.

Describe a house near an interstate ramp or rail line candidly, because noise tends to come up at showings. Easy road access is still a plus for commuters, so mention both.

Neighborhoods and buyer types

Columbia has many named neighborhoods, and each draws its own crowd. Arsenal Hill and Congaree Vista sit near downtown. Elmwood Park, the Waverly Historic District, Granby Mill Village and Rosewood are older, close-in areas. Five Points, Old Shandon and University Hill lie near the University of South Carolina, where rental demand shapes the market.

Investors tend to look near downtown and the campus, especially at houses with tenants already in place. A family buyer is more likely to want move-in condition, which is why a worn house in the same neighborhood can sit. Tell a cash buyer about any tenants, lease end dates and the rental permit status up front, since those details change what the house is worth to them.

Your options for a quick sale

Three routes are open to a Columbia seller: hire an agent, go it alone, or accept a cash offer. Houses near the university or downtown often draw investors. Houses that need work, or that have tenants in place, are harder to sell on the open market.

Here is how the paths differ in practice:

  • Agent listing suits a house in good shape when waiting out showings, inspections and a buyer's loan approval is acceptable.
  • Selling yourself saves the commission but puts pricing, paperwork and negotiation on you.
  • A cash offer is normally as-is: no repair requests, no lender, and often a closing date of your choosing.

Collect four items before deciding: rental permit status, the county for your parcel, your latest tax bill and the payoff on your mortgage. Buyers and closing attorneys ask about all four.

What happens from offer to closing

Every sale moves through the same stages, but the clock differs. You accept a price and sign a purchase contract. The buyer then checks the property: inspection, title search and, if there is a loan, an appraisal. Cash buyers can often trim or drop the appraisal and lender stages, and those stages cause most of the slippage in a normal sale.

An attorney drafts the deed and settlement statement. At the table you sign, the attorney sends payoff money to your lender and clears any unpaid taxes from the proceeds, and the deed gets recorded. Whatever remains is yours.

Take a photo ID, your lender's name and loan number, keys and garage remotes, plus any leases and rental permit papers. A co-owner or heir named on the title must sign as well, so arrange that early. A lien or back taxes will not block a sale because they come out of the proceeds, but request payoff numbers well ahead of closing.

Little jobs help. Empty the rooms so inspectors can reach everything. Collect receipts for roof, HVAC or plumbing work to answer questions quickly. Keep utilities on in your name until closing day so the inspector can test the systems.

Frequently asked questions

Is Columbia in Richland County?

Mostly. Columbia is the Richland County seat, but parts of the city reach into Lexington and Kershaw counties. Confirm your parcel's county before you call an assessor or treasurer.

Do I need a rental permit to sell a rented house in Columbia?

The city requires a Residential Rental Permit for each rental unit, renewed every year by December 31. A buyer will want proof it is current. Code Enforcement can help at 803-545-4362.

When are Richland County property taxes due?

Payment is due between September 30 and January 15. A 3 percent penalty starts after January 15. Ask the treasurer for the exact date and amount on your notice.

How long do I have to appeal a Columbia assessment?

You have 90 days from the dated reassessment notice, or until the first penalty date on the current bill if that comes first. An appeal does not stop the bill from coming due.

Can a buyer use a Columbia house as an Airbnb?

Only where zoning and the city permit allow it. An STR Permit and a Business License are both required. In residential areas it depends on the street or on owner occupancy under the 2026 ordinance.

Older neighborhoods and housing age

The city grew around the Charleston Naval Shipyard, established in 1901, and the Naval Base that ran from 1902 to 1996. Park Circle was one of the first areas planned, in 1912, with industrial, commercial and residential sections. At incorporation the city took in Russelldale, Ferndale, Morningside, Liberty Park, Palmetto Heights, Singing Pines, Dewey Hill, Liberty Homes and John C. Calhoun Homes.

Older neighborhoods can come with aging wiring, plumbing and roofs, and a financed buyer's inspector will raise them. A cash sale does not require you to make those repairs first.

Flood questions that come up in a sale

Standing water and tidal flooding are the bigger worry in the Lowcountry. Charleston County's flood flyer urges homeowners to learn their flood zone, flood depth and flood history, because ordinary homeowners insurance generally leaves flood damage uncovered.

  • When the house is in a Special Flood Hazard Area and the mortgage is federally backed, flood insurance is required.
  • Elevation affects the premium, so an agent may ask for an elevation certificate.

How long the trip is to the airport, the port or the base can shift what a street is worth, and a local agent can speak to that for your neighborhood.

City offices for permits and code

The city's own pages cover Code Enforcement, Business Licenses, Zoning with an online map, Building Inspections and a Certificate of Occupancy page. If you have done work without a permit, or an open violation sits on the house, learn that before a buyer's attorney does.

Property taxes and assessments

Your parcel's county does the assessing. Houses in the Charleston County slice of the city follow Charleston County rules, while parcels in Berkeley or Dorchester follow theirs.

Inside Charleston County, the house you live in is assessed at 4 percent and every other kind of real estate at 6 percent. Multiply assessed value by the millage and you have the tax; a mill is a thousandth of a dollar. Residents must ask for the lower ratio by filing an application, ideally early in the year.

State law lets you pay from September 30 through January 15. Once that date is behind you, penalties of 3, 7 and 5 percent begin. August is when reassessment notices go out, and the county will quote the current appeal deadline. A sale or transfer is the one case that escapes the 15 percent cap, so the next owner's bill can differ from yours.

Real estate questions go to the county Auditor at (843) 958-4234 or RealProperty@CharlestonCounty.org. Ask whether any balance is open before you set a closing date, since the title company will want it settled.

A Charleston County deed is filed downtown at the Register of Deeds, 101 Meeting Street, Suite 200. The office opens at 8:30 a.m., closes at 5:00 p.m. on weekdays and answers at (843) 958-4800. If your house is in the Berkeley or Dorchester part of the city, the deed is recorded by that county.

Expect a state deed fee of $1.85 for every $500 of value, with an exception for estate distribution deeds. Your closing attorney can list the exact documents and affidavits your transfer requires.

Disclosure and inherited houses

A written disclosure statement is what South Carolina asks of an owner, unless the sale is exempt. Transfers by a fiduciary who administers an estate, guardianship or trust are exempt, which helps an executor selling a parent's home. Heirs selling in their own names may not qualify, and an attorney can confirm. As-is deals are also permitted by the same law.

Planning your timeline

Three things set the pace of a sale here: which county holds the parcel, whether anything is owed on the house and whether the title is clear. Start with the county, since that tells you which offices to call for a tax balance and which Register of Deeds will record the deed.

Then ask for a payoff on any mortgage and a current figure for taxes. If the house is in an estate, confirm who has authority to sign. With those answers in hand, a closing date is simple to set, and surprises are rare.

Selling an occupied or rental house

A tenant in place or an empty rental makes a traditional listing slow. Showings are hard to schedule, and a buyer using a loan expects a clean house in good condition. For those owners, comparing a cash sale of an occupied house against listing is worthwhile.

Round up the lease, the rent records and notes on repairs the tenant has requested, and be ready to describe the tenant's situation plainly.

How a cash sale works

Our team at Cash Home Buyers visits North Charleston houses wherever they stand today and writes any offer down. Whether one comes depends on the property.

If you agree, the closing date is yours to pick. No appraisal gets ordered since no bank is lending. Title work, payoffs from your proceeds and the deed filing all go through a closing attorney or title company.

To get ready, locate the newest tax bill, a mortgage payoff figure and, for inherited property, the estate papers. Name the county on the first call so the recording can be planned.

Keep your copy of the settlement statement afterward. It shows what was paid out and is the record you will want at tax time.

Where do I record a deed for a Charleston County house in North Charleston?

Charleston County parcels go to the county Register of Deeds, 101 Meeting Street, Suite 200, Charleston. Berkeley and Dorchester parcels are recorded in their own counties.

Do I have to disclose problems if I inherited the house?

Probably not if you are an executor or other fiduciary handling the estate, since South Carolina exempts that transfer. Heirs selling in their own names may need to give the statement, so check with an attorney.

Is flood insurance required to sell a North Charleston house?

Not for you as the seller. The buyer needs it when the house is in a Special Flood Hazard Area and the mortgage is federally backed, and the policy usually takes 30 days to start.

Mount Pleasant at a glance

Older homes and the Old Village

People settled here in 1680, and the name Mount Pleasant came in 1803. The Hibben House, built in 1755, is called the town's oldest home.

Housing ranges widely. The Old Village, centered on the Pitt Street Shops, is the oldest neighborhood, and its historic district appears on the National Register of Historic Places. Scanlonville grew from an early African American community founded after the Civil War and has since been annexed. Riverside opened in 1930 and is now a gated community.

If you own an older house near the Old Village, ask the Town of Mount Pleasant's planning staff whether exterior repairs need review before you spend money.

Flood risk and your sale

Sitting low beside tidal water, Mount Pleasant puts flood status near the top of every buyer's and lender's list. These points from Charleston County's flood flyer tend to come up at closing:

  • A flood policy typically takes effect 30 days after purchase.
  • Agents sometimes want an elevation certificate. A surveyor, engineer or architect can prepare one when the town has none on file.

Phone the Town to ask which flood zone your parcel falls in and whether it already has an elevation certificate on file. Having that paper in hand heads off a delay.

Schools, bridges and roads

Charleston County School District runs the public schools, so the first question from many buyers is which zone a house sits in. Wando High School opened in 1973. The town also has Lucy Garrett Beckham High School and Oceanside Collegiate Academy, plus middle schools named Laing, Moultrie and Thomas Cario. Check the district's address lookup rather than a listing description.

The Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge, an eight-lane cable-stayed span that opened July 16, 2005, carries U.S. 17 over the Cooper River into Charleston. Charleston International Airport is about 12 miles northwest, and Mount Pleasant Regional Airport (Faison Field) lies inside the town limits.

Recording a deed in Charleston County

Filing happens downtown at the Charleston County Register of Deeds, 101 Meeting Street, Suite 200. Weekday hours run 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., but anything delivered by hand after 4:30 p.m. will not be taken. The phone is (843) 958-4800, and the staff cannot coach you through the forms.

For the next owner it does. The county revalues a qualifying sale at market value as of December 31 of that year and drops the 15% cap. A buyer who will live there has to apply separately for the 4% rate.
